PCOS is the most common cause of both delayed menarche and persistent, treatment-refractory acne in adolescents; its prevalence, typical age of presentation (menarche often delayed to 15–16 years), and association with ovarian androgen excess make it the leading diagnosis. Non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency) is a close second—often presents with precocious pubarche, acne, and oligo/amenorrhea due to adrenal androgen overproduction; it may be underdiagnosed without targeted testing. Hyperprolactinemia can suppress GnRH pulsatility, delaying menarche, and is associated with acne via indirect effects on ovarian androgen production and altered sex hormone binding globulin; however, galactorrhea or headache would increase suspicion. Hypothalamic amenorrhea is less likely without clear behavioral triggers (e.g., excessive exercise, low weight, stress), but functional hypothalamic suppression can manifest with acne due to relative hyperandrogenemia from low SHBG and unopposed ovarian androgen secretion. Turner syndrome (45,X) is included due to primary amenorrhea, but severe acne is atypical—more commonly associated with estrogen deficiency, short stature, and lack of secondary sexual development; thus, confidence is lower unless other stigmata are present."}
